ideas.author: Samuel Butler
ideas.judged: AI models could not judge when it may arrive
ideas.line: Machines gradually evolving an inner awareness of their own, much as living species once did.
ideas.name: Mechanical Consciousness
ideas.profit: not judged (not a technology, not something sold, not physically possible, or unclear)

verdict.money_why: Nothing is sold, so nobody pays and no seller keeps anything.
verdict.prize_why: Machines slowly growing aware is something that happens in the story and not a product.

ideas.arrival: built in the 1970s, about 100 years after it was imagined
ideas.author: Edward Page Mitchell
ideas.line: A household machine that produces a paper copy of whichever newspaper you pick, sent over a wire.
ideas.name: Home News Printer

verdict.money_why: Readers pay for the machine and the paper they pick, the machine is easy to copy, and the newspapers that own the news collect.
verdict.prize_why: Printing the paper at home saves a delivery and is a convenience for readers.

ideas.author: Edward Page Mitchell
ideas.judged: AI models' likeliest decade: 2100 or later
ideas.line: Freezing a living person so the body can be stored for years and later revived.
ideas.name: Suspended Animation (Frigorific Process)
ideas.profit: a fat profit, kept by the maker

verdict.money_why: I assumed carriers and hospitals buy it; the method could be copied once known, so the firms that already run ships and hospitals collect.
verdict.prize_why: Putting people safely into long dormancy would make very long journeys possible and give hospitals time to treat the gravely ill.

ideas.arrival: built in 1943, 68 years after it was imagined
ideas.author: Jules Verne
ideas.line: Self-contained breathing gear that lets a person roam around the ocean floor for hours.
ideas.name: Diving Apparatus

verdict.money_why: I assume sport divers are the main buyers, and many firms can make tanks and valves, so no seller keeps much.
verdict.prize_why: Breathing gear for roaming the sea floor opened diving for sport, salvage and science, which is a real but modest trade.

ideas.author: Jules Verne
ideas.line: A large, self-sufficient electric submarine able to roam the oceans for long periods without surfacing.
ideas.name: Nautilus
ideas.profit: a fat profit, kept by the maker

verdict.money_why: I assume navies are the main buyers, and the shipyards that already hold naval contracts collect.
verdict.prize_why: A submarine that stays under for long periods and feeds itself is worth a great deal to a navy and an industry to those who build it.

ideas.author: Edward Page Mitchell
ideas.judged: AI models judge it not physically possible
ideas.line: A machine that breaks an object down in one place and reassembles it somewhere else.
ideas.name: Telepomp (Matter Transmission)
ideas.profit: not judged (not a technology, not something sold, not physically possible, or unclear)

verdict.money_why: Traders and carriers pay, since the description sends objects and not people, which is why the payer differs from the booths for travellers; once a firm had built it others could, so the carriers and builders that already own the depots and the customers collect.
verdict.prize_why: Sending things instantly across any distance would replace most shipping and haulage, which changes how most people are supplied and how most firms work.

ideas.arrival: built in the 1960s, about 90 years after it was imagined
ideas.author: Jules Verne
ideas.line: Extracting metals and minerals from deposits lying on the deep ocean bottom.
ideas.name: Undersea Mining
ideas.profit: a monopoly-like profit, kept by licence holders

verdict.money_why: Metal users buy the ore, and many could build the gear, so mining firms with ships, money and seabed claims collect; I assumed claims are not scarce.
verdict.prize_why: Metals from the deep ocean floor would add a great new supply for industry.

ideas.author: Jules Verne
ideas.line: Charging a vessel's metal skin with high voltage so anyone who touches it gets shocked.
ideas.name: Electrify the Rail

verdict.money_why: Assuming shipowners fit it against boarders, any marine electrician can do the work.
verdict.prize_why: Charging a hull to shock boarders is a simple trick for a few vessels.

ideas.author: Jules Verne
ideas.line: A projectile for undersea hunting that stuns or kills its target with a strong electric discharge.
ideas.name: Leyden Ball

verdict.money_why: Hunters and divers buy it, and a charged dart is simple enough that many workshops could make it, so no seller keeps much.
verdict.prize_why: An electric projectile for hunting under the sea serves a small group of divers and fishers.

ideas.author: Edward Page Mitchell
ideas.judged: AI models judge it not physically possible
ideas.line: A single tiny tablet holding enough nourishment to feed a person for weeks.
ideas.name: Compact Food Pastilles
ideas.profit: not judged (not a technology, not something sold, not physically possible, or unclear)

verdict.money_why: Households buy it, and I assumed the recipe can be copied once it is known, so the food and pharmacy brands with shop space collect.
verdict.prize_why: Judged as if it worked, one tablet that feeds a person for weeks would be an industry of its own and would change how armies, travellers and the hungry are fed, though I assumed most people would still eat ordinary meals for pleasure.

ideas.author: Edward Bulwer-Lytton
ideas.line: Using the scarce remains of a vanished sea creature as currency whose value rests on limited supply.
ideas.name: Fossil Shell Coin
ideas.profit: not judged (not a technology, not something sold, not physically possible, or unclear)

verdict.money_why: Nothing is sold, so nobody pays and no seller keeps anything.
verdict.prize_why: Using scarce old shells as money is a custom, and the shells are found, not made.
